verified_ref: Vairagyashatakam 82 in the popular Nirnaya Sagar / Chaukhamba numbering (GRETIL 3.82; Madhavananda 1916 no. 82); Wortham 1886 no. 51; Kale 1902 no. 49; Kosambi 1948 no. 308 (in his 'doubtful verses' block).
attribution_note: Traditional attribution stands, but Kosambi's critical edition prints it among the doubtful verses (201-352), i.e. it is not in the core shared by all recensions.
translation_note: Minor: 'for long' belongs to the poet's reflection, not to the mind looking outward. Kale, Wortham and Madhavananda all read it as 'though I have pondered it for a long time, I do not know what noble austerity has ripened into this', with the mind described as stirring only slowly toward outer things. Suggested fix: '...a mind that moves only slowly toward outer things. Though I have pondered it long, I cannot tell what noble austerity has ripened into this.' The 'line' paraphrase is fine.
context: Late in the Vairagyashatakam the poet has just said that moonlight, poetry and good company all lose their charm once the mind sees how fleeting they are, and that the wise leave palaces for the forest. Here he lists the goods of the renunciant's life and marvels at them as the ripened fruit of some great austerity. The verses that follow turn to devotion to Shiva, including the one declaring Shiva and Vishnu not different in essence.

key_terms.sense: moving about at one's own will; freedom of the wandering life
food that costs no self-abasement (no fawning on the rich for it)
living in the company of noble people
(learning) whose sole fruit is the vow of inner calm
the ripening of some noble austerity

core_teaching: A plain, self-respecting life (free movement, honest food, good company, study aimed at calm, a quiet mind) is treated as a rare blessing, the ripened fruit of great effort, to be wondered at rather than taken for granted.

commentaries.who: Swami Madhavananda, translation with notes (Advaita Ashrama 1916, no. 82)
commentaries.gist: Glosses upaśama as the ending of the world's illusions and worries; says this is the only fruit of such study, whereas other vows promise worldly prosperity. Renders the close as the poet unable, even after lifelong reflection, to name the austerity behind it.

commentaries.who: M. R. Kale, translation (1902 ed., Vairagya 49)
commentaries.gist: Takes the long reflection as the poet's own, and describes the mind as moving only slowly toward external objects; the learning's fruit is the vow of sense-control.

commentaries.who: B. Hale Wortham, translation (1886, Vairagya 51)
commentaries.gist: Lists rest at will, food without degradation, friendship with the noble-minded and an undisturbed mind as fruits of the highest vow of tranquillity, then admits he cannot tell what penance wins this state.

commentaries.who: D. D. Kosambi, critical edition (1948, no. 308)
commentaries.gist: Places the verse in the doubtful block; his text reads 'bahir aticirasyāpi', confirming the long-reflection reading.

practical_reading: Read as a gratitude exercise: name the ordinary freedoms and dignities you already have (choosing your own hours, food you did not have to beg for, good friends, a mind that is not racing) and notice them as gifts rather than entitlements.
misreadings: Not a boast that one has earned one's comforts; the tone is wonder, not desert.
Not praise of luxury; the goods listed are those of a simple, even ascetic, life.
Not a claim that people lacking these goods failed to earn them.
cautions: The 'fruit of past austerity' frame can imply that hardship is deserved; avoid for a reader in poverty, dependency or humiliating work.
Original context is the renunciant's life, not a householder's comforts.
speaks_to: appreciating good company and a calm mind
not_for: someone who has just lost their freedom, job or home
someone forced to depend on others for food or money
research_note: Plan data: gratitude day 1 still carries the heading 'The taste in water', which belonged to the replaced bg.7.8. Section label 'Worship of Shiva' follows popular editions; Madhavananda's text has no section headings, but verses 83-84 there are indeed Shiva devotion.

verified_ref: Complete Works, Vol. 5, Epistles - First Series, letter CIII, to Mary Hale, from the Math, Belur, 18 May 1901. Page number not checked.
translation_note: The first and last sentences checked verbatim against the CW text online; the middle sentence matches the letter's sense (gloomy mood, wretched health).
context: Vivekananda had returned to India in December 1900 and spent spring 1901 touring East Bengal and Assam; after about two months of hard travel he collapsed and came back to Calcutta to recover. The letter opens with a joke about Mary's letter wandering the world, then reports the Raja of Khetri's death and his own poor health, says he would like to go to Europe for a long talk with her, and claims three-quarters of his restlessness has gone. He closes with love to friends and lifelong gratitude to Mary's mother.

key_terms.sense: to resurface like a float; to recover after going under
the next turn of fortune's wheel
his plain naming of grief and illness

core_teaching: Not a doctrine but an honest note from a teacher at a low point: he names grief and illness without disguise and still expects the tide to turn.

commentaries.who: Context of the letter (Complete Works vol. 5, letter CIII)
commentaries.gist: Written after a strenuous East Bengal and Assam tour left him collapsed; the bad news and the expectation of recovery sit in one short paragraph between banter and affectionate greetings.

commentaries.who: Raja Ajit Singh of Khetri (Wikipedia)
commentaries.gist: Died 18 January 1901 at Sikandra near Agra when a tower he stood on collapsed. He had funded Vivekananda's 1893 voyage, suggested the name 'Vivekananda', and sent a monthly stipend to his mother.

commentaries.who: Vivekananda's last years (Wikipedia)
commentaries.gist: From 1901 his asthma, diabetes and insomnia limited him; he died at Belur Math on 4 July 1902, about fourteen months after this letter.

practical_reading: You can say plainly that things are bad right now and, in the same breath, decide to wait for the turn rather than conclude it will never come.
misreadings: Not a promise that health or fortune will return on schedule.
Not a brush-off of grief; he names the loss first.
cautions: Mentions an accidental death (the Raja's fall).
His health did not recover; he died the following year. Do not frame 'bob up' as a guarantee, especially for a reader who is seriously ill.
speaks_to: a low patch after loss plus illness
losing hope but not giving up
being honest about a bad season
not_for: someone with a terminal diagnosis, if read as a promise of recovery
very fresh bereavement where 'bob up soon' may feel rushed
research_note: Plan data: in losing-hope day 2 the heading 'Stand up' belonged to the replaced bg.2.3 and no longer fits this letter.

verified_ref: Complete Works, Vol. 1, Karma-Yoga, chapter VII 'Freedom' (New York class talks; vivekananda.net's lecture list dates 'Freedom' to 10 January 1896). Page 101 not checked.
translation_note: Both sentences checked verbatim (vivekananda.net text of the chapter). In the original the first line is in quotation marks and presented as Karma-Yoga's own teaching, not as a quote from a named scripture.
context: In 'Freedom' Vivekananda says the whole universe is struggling toward freedom and that Karma-Yoga is the science of working well. He then gives this line as Karma-Yoga's message, illustrated by two burned paintings: a stranger's loss barely touches us, but losing our own painting hurts because we have made it 'mine'. He follows with the lotus leaf that sits in water without getting wet, and two routes to non-attachment: self-reliance for those without belief in God, offering the fruits of work to God for believers.

key_terms.sense: treating the work or its results as 'mine'
being in the work without being soaked by it
the discipline of work done freely, without clinging to results

core_teaching: Work itself does not make us miserable; our identification with it and its results does. Work wholeheartedly, but hold the outcome as not 'mine'.

commentaries.who: Surrounding text (Complete Works vol. 1, Karma-Yoga ch. VII)
commentaries.gist: The burned-painting example: the same loss hurts only when it is ours; 'mine' extends to house, children and body. Advises enjoying things without claiming them.

commentaries.who: Same chapter, later paragraphs
commentaries.gist: Non-attachment is the basis of all the yogas: a person in a cave can be attached and a king free. Duty becomes a burden when it hardens into compulsion; act freely and expect no praise, like the many unknown people who work silently.

commentaries.who: Lecture chronology (vivekananda.net)
commentaries.gist: Lists 'Freedom' among the New York Karma-Yoga talks, dated 10 January 1896.

practical_reading: When work is draining you, look for where you have fused your worth with the outcome; keep doing the task well but loosen the 'this must go my way' grip.
misreadings: Not 'stop caring about your work'.
Not a denial that workload, poor conditions or exploitation cause real exhaustion.
cautions: For genuine burnout from overwork, 'it is your attachment' can sound like blame; acknowledge the load first.
speaks_to: work that has become your identity
not_for: someone exhausted by unsafe or exploitative conditions who needs to change the conditions
research_note: The ramakrishnavivekananda.info page for this chapter returned a bot-check screen, so verification used vivekananda.net's text of the same chapter.

verified_ref: Vairagyashatakam 61 in popular numbering (GRETIL 3.61; Madhavananda 1916 no. 61); Wortham 1886 no. 34; Kale 1902 no. 33; Kosambi 1948 no. 167 (core verse).
attribution_note: In Kosambi's core of 200 verses common to all recensions.
translation_note: Acceptable. Text variant worth knowing: Kosambi's critical text reads 'cintāmaṇi-guṇe vimukteḥ saṅkalpaḥ' (the resolve toward liberation) where the popular text has 'cintāmaṇi-gaṇo viviktaḥ saṅkalpaḥ' (a secluded / unentangled resolve). Madhavananda renders vivikta as 'free from the company of others', i.e. not dependent on others; 'clear' in our translation is a fair gloss.
context: The poet turns from describing kings and ascetics to addressing his own heart. He asks why it wears itself out courting other people's favour every day, and answers that a mind serene within already holds a wish-granting jewel. Nearby verses rebuke the mind for roaming everywhere except inward.

key_terms.sense: propitiating / courting other people's minds
a mass of trouble; what the heart walks into
when you are serene within
the mythical wish-granting gem
a resolve kept apart, not dependent on others

core_teaching: Approval chased from others is exhausting and unreliable; a mind settled within is itself the source of what one is looking for.

commentaries.who: Swami Madhavananda, translation with notes (1916, no. 61)
commentaries.gist: Notes the alternative reading kleśa-kalitam ('a chaotic mass of troubles'); explains the self-arisen wish-gem as almost a yogic power, and takes vivikta as being free of the need for others' company.

commentaries.who: M. R. Kale, translation (1902 ed., Vairagya 33)
commentaries.gist: Renders it as the heart suffering much distress to please others daily, whereas when wish-gem powers rise in it spontaneously and it is inwardly satisfied, nothing desired is out of reach.

commentaries.who: B. Hale Wortham, translation (1886, Vairagya 34)
commentaries.gist: Reads the point as: a purified heart would have its desires met and would stop seeking others' favours because it would be at rest inside.

commentaries.who: D. D. Kosambi, critical edition (1948, no. 167)
commentaries.gist: Core verse; critical text points the resolve toward liberation (vimukti) rather than toward seclusion.

practical_reading: Notice how much daily energy goes into managing other people's opinion of you, and try one stretch of the day where you act from your own settled sense of what is right rather than from the wish to be liked.
misreadings: Not permission to ignore other people's needs or feedback.
Not 'manifesting': the wish-gem is inner contentment, not a guarantee of external outcomes.
cautions: For a carer or employee who cannot stop pleasing others without real cost, the verse can sound like blame; frame it as relief, not fault.
not_for: someone whose safety depends on placating another person (abuse, coercive work); they need practical help, not an inner-calm verse

verified_ref: Vairagyashatakam 44 in popular numbering (GRETIL 3.44; Madhavananda 1916 no. 44); Wortham 1886 no. 78 (= Telang 78); Kale 1902 no. 75; Kosambi 1948 no. 316 (doubtful block).
attribution_note: Kosambi prints it among the doubtful verses (201-352), so it is outside the core common to all recensions.
translation_note: Good. Small textual variant: Kosambi reads 'punar-ukta-bhukta-viṣayaiḥ' (the same objects enjoyed again and again), which is how Wortham translates it; the popular text has 'bhūta'.
context: Part of the run of verses on Time in the Vairagyashatakam: just before, the poet says life shrinks with each sunrise and sunset while business hides the passing of time, and that the world has gone mad on the wine of delusion. Here he observes people treating each day as a repeat of the last and pursuing the same routines without ever feeling ashamed of the treadmill.

key_terms.term: rātriḥ saiva punaḥ sa eva divasaḥ
key_terms.sense: it is the same night again, the same day
they run about busily
repeated, said over again (stale)
harassed / made a fool of by worldly life
out of delusion we feel no shame

core_teaching: Treating life as an endless loop of identical days lets it slip away unnoticed; the verse asks us to wake up to the repetition and to time passing.

commentaries.who: Swami Madhavananda, translation with notes (1916, no. 44)
commentaries.gist: Explains that desire, which never ages, makes stale pursuits look fresh; in truth worldly pursuits are as repetitive as day following night.

commentaries.who: M. R. Kale, translation (1902 ed., Vairagya 75)
commentaries.gist: Renders it as ignorant people busily running their diverse vocations, and asks why we are not ashamed of being disgraced by such repetitive worldly life.

commentaries.who: B. Hale Wortham, translation (1886, Vairagya 78)
commentaries.gist: Stresses that we assume days and nights go on indefinitely, resume each task where we left it, and endure the world's pains while enjoying the same sense-objects over and over.

commentaries.who: D. D. Kosambi, critical edition (1948, no. 316)
commentaries.gist: Doubtful-block verse; critical text reads the 'enjoyed again' variant.

practical_reading: When the week feels like a loop, stop and ask what this particular day is for; change one small thing so it is not simply a rerun of yesterday.
misreadings: Not contempt for ordinary work or routine as such; the target is mindless repetition driven by craving.
Not a call to quit one's responsibilities.
cautions: The 'we feel no shame' language can shame someone already depleted; many people repeat exhausting routines out of necessity, not delusion.
Includes the poet himself ('we'); keep that inclusive tone.
speaks_to: feeling like a hamster on a wheel
not_for: someone trapped in a routine by caregiving or poverty who would hear it as an accusation
someone with depression for whom 'same day again' is a symptom, not a choice
research_note: Telang's 1874 edition also numbers it 78 (seen in the OCR of that edition), matching Wortham.

verified_ref: Complete Works, Vol. 4, Writings: Poems, 'Hold On Yet a While, Brave Heart' (subtitled as written to H. H. the Maharaja of Khetri, Rajputana). No date given on the CW page; page numbers not checked.
translation_note: All quoted lines checked verbatim. The excerpt joins stanza 1 and stanza 4 with ellipses; note stanza 4 says 'brave soul', not 'brave heart'.
context: A six-stanza poem of encouragement to Ajit Singh, Raja of Khetri, Vivekananda's friend and patron. It moves from the clouded sun, through winter always followed by summer, heavy duties and fleeting pleasures, to the claim that no honest work is lost; a fifth stanza tells the wise few to guide the many gently, and the last promises help from those who see far and from the Lord.

key_terms.sense: endure a little longer; the refrain
the sky (old poetic word)
no good action is ever wasted or cancelled

core_teaching: Dark stretches alternate with light ones, and sincere effort is never wasted even when hopes fail, so keep going a little longer.

commentaries.who: Surrounding text: the whole poem (Complete Works vol. 4)
commentaries.gist: Stanza 2 adds that winter is always followed by summer and life alternates like waves; stanza 4 that no work or struggle is lost though hopes and strength fail; stanza 5 is advice to a leader of the masses.

commentaries.who: Addressee: Ajit Singh of Khetri (Wikipedia)
commentaries.gist: Ruler of Khetri who financed Vivekananda's 1893 voyage and supported his mother; the poem is addressed to a powerful friend and patron, not to a stranger in crisis.

commentaries.who: vivekananda.net text of the poem
commentaries.gist: Gives the same six stanzas with no date or circumstances of composition; the date remains unestablished in the sources checked.

practical_reading: On a day when work feels shaky, take the poem as permission to stay steady for one more stretch while remembering that effort is not wasted even if this particular outcome fails.
misreadings: Not a guarantee of a specific outcome ('victory is sure' is poetic encouragement).
Not advice to stay in a harmful or dangerous workplace.
cautions: In a plan called 'When work feels unsafe', 'hold on' must not read as 'put up with harassment, danger or abuse'. If unsafe means unsafe, the right step is to get help or leave.
Stanza 5 has an elitist ring (the wise few guiding the masses); avoid quoting it out of context.
not_for: workplace harassment or physical danger
someone who has already held on too long and needs permission to stop
research_note: Date of composition not found in CW or vivekananda.net.

verified_ref: Nitishatakam 58 in popular, Wortham 1886 and Kale 1902 numbering (GRETIL 1.58); Kosambi 1948 no. 35 (core verse). Wortham notes it also occurs in the Hitopadesha (Mitrabheda 25).
attribution_note: Core verse in Kosambi, but it is a shared gnomic verse also found in the Hitopadesha.
translation_note: Good and close to Kale. Wortham generalises sevādharma to 'the laws by which behaviour is regulated', but the Sanskrit means the code of service to a master, as our translation has it. The 'line' ('harder than yoga') slightly shifts the point: the verse says even yogis, with their insight, cannot fathom it. Suggest: 'Even yogis can't master serving a boss.'
context: From the Nitishatakam's group of verses on wicked or difficult people (Wortham's section 52-61). Just before, the poet lists 'seven thorns' in his heart, including a wicked man at court, and warns that an angry king has no friends. This verse describes the courtier's or servant's trap: every way of behaving is twisted into a fault.

key_terms.sense: silent, so called dumb
articulate, so called crazy or a chatterer
pushy (if near) / timid (if distant)
the code of serving a master
beyond the reach even of yogis

core_teaching: When you serve someone powerful, any behaviour can be read as a fault; the problem lies in the position, not necessarily in you.

commentaries.who: M. R. Kale, translation and notes (1902 ed., Niti 58)
commentaries.gist: Calls service the hardest thing even for sages; notes that yogis are credited with superhuman insight through contemplation, yet even they cannot fathom it; 'apragalbha' means timid.

commentaries.who: B. Hale Wortham, translation and notes (1886, Niti 58)
commentaries.gist: Renders it as rules of behaviour impossible to learn even for an ascetic, and records that the verse also appears in the Hitopadesha.

commentaries.who: D. D. Kosambi, critical edition (1948, no. 35)
commentaries.gist: Core verse; same text in substance ('dhṛṣṭaḥ pārśve...').

practical_reading: If every choice you make at work gets criticised, recognise the double bind for what it is; stop trying to find the one 'right' behaviour and anchor in your own standard.
misreadings: Not a claim that all feedback from a manager is unfair.
Not advice to stop trying; it describes a structural bind.
cautions: Can feed cynicism about authority if used alone; pair with a constructive step.
speaks_to: feeling nothing you do is right at work
being judged whichever way you act
not_for: someone receiving fair, specific feedback they need to hear

verified_ref: Nitishatakam 54 (GRETIL 1.54; Wortham 1886 and Kale 1902 also 54); Kosambi 1948 no. 24 (core verse).
translation_note: Good. Nuances: 'muni' here, per Kale, is a reserved or silent person, so 'the quiet sage is called slow' is closer than 'thoughtful sage'; Kosambi's critical text reads 'ṛjau' (the straightforward person) instead of 'munau'. 'Aśaktiḥ sthire' is 'the steady person is called incapable / feeble', as ours has it.
context: In the Nitishatakam's section on the wicked: right after the advice to avoid a learned but wicked man (53), the poet catalogues how spiteful people re-label each virtue as its nearest vice, and ends asking which virtue they have not stained.

key_terms.sense: in the modest person they see dullness
hypocrisy / fraud (what devotion and purity are called)
in the gentle speaker they see servility
not branded by the wicked

core_teaching: Malicious critics can turn any virtue into a fault by renaming it; their verdict says more about them than about the person judged.

commentaries.who: M. R. Kale, translation and notes (1902 ed., Niti 54)
commentaries.gist: Explains that 'is counted as' must be supplied in each clause, and that muni here means a reserved, silent person; the verse asks what virtue the wicked have not stigmatised.

commentaries.who: B. Hale Wortham, translation and notes (1886, Niti 54)
commentaries.gist: Focuses on 'aṅkitaḥ', branded: the good's virtues are branded as vices by the evil-minded; compares a Greek proverb on the same idea.

commentaries.who: D. D. Kosambi, critical edition (1948, no. 24)
commentaries.gist: Core verse; reads 'ṛjau vimatitā' (the honest are called stupid).

practical_reading: When someone's criticism of you is just your strength described unkindly (your calm called coldness, your care called weakness), name the trick and stop absorbing it.
misreadings: Not every criticism is spite; it is a tool for recognising malice, not for dismissing fair feedback.
cautions: Avoid encouraging the reader to label everyone who criticises them as wicked.
not_for: someone who needs to hear honest correction

verified_ref: Vairagyashatakam 4 in popular numbering (GRETIL 3.4; Madhavananda 1916 no. 4); Wortham 1886 no. 6; Kale 1902 no. 6; Kosambi 1948 no. 150 (core verse).
translation_note: Good. 'Āśā' is rendered variously: hope (ours), desire (Wortham, Madhavananda), greed (Kale). 'Futile hope' for 'moghāśe' is fine; a few manuscripts read 'amoghāśe' (Kosambi apparatus).
context: Early in the Vairagyashatakam's censure of craving: in the preceding verses the poet confesses digging for treasure, smelting ore, crossing seas and humbling himself before kings, all fruitless. Here he lists the humiliations he swallowed to win favour and asks hope or desire how much longer it will make him dance. The next verse in popular editions continues the confession: for the sake of a life as unstable as water on a lotus leaf, he shamelessly recited his own merits before the rich.

key_terms.sense: the taunts of the wicked, endured
holding back the tears inside
laughing with an empty mind
the stupor / stiffness that wealth brings
O hope, vain hope, you make me dance

core_teaching: Unexamined hope for gain or approval can make us swallow insults and fake our feelings; naming that pattern is the first step out of it.

commentaries.who: Swami Madhavananda, translation (1916, no. 4)
commentaries.gist: Places it in servile attendance on wealthy wicked people: shabby treatment borne, tears suppressed, forced smiles, bows to men dulled by wealth; addresses Desire, whose yearning is never satisfied.

commentaries.who: M. R. Kale, translation (1902 ed., Vairagya 6)
commentaries.gist: Renders the addressee as 'disappointed Greed' and stresses enduring taunts while intent on propitiating the powerful.

commentaries.who: B. Hale Wortham, translation (1886, Vairagya 6)
commentaries.gist: Frames the abuse as suffered in hope of gain, the laughter as forced from a void heart, and asks foolish desire how much further it will lead him.

practical_reading: Notice what you put up with because you hope it will pay off (the promotion, the approval); ask whether that hope is still worth the price you are paying in self-respect.
misreadings: Not a condemnation of all hope; it targets the hope that keeps one in humiliation.
Not a judgement on people who must endure a bad job to survive.
cautions: Describes suppressed tears and forced laughter; can land heavily on someone in an abusive workplace. Avoid implying their hope is the problem.
not_for: someone with no option to leave a degrading situation, unless paired with practical support

verified_ref: Complete Works, Vol. 3, Lectures from Colombo to Almora, 'My Plan of Campaign', delivered at the Victoria (Public) Hall, Madras; vivekananda.net's lecture list dates it 9 February 1897. Page 208 not checked.
translation_note: Opening sentence and 'as soon as he dares to differ' checked verbatim; the rest of the excerpt matches the passage's sense.
context: Speaking in Madras after his return from the West, Vivekananda first addresses the Theosophical Society: Hindus are grateful for its work and he respects Mrs Besant, but respect does not mean accepting everything, and he denies the rumour that Theosophists helped his success in America. This passage then observes that 'sympathy' lasts only while one agrees. He goes on to describe how Theosophists and some Christian missionaries opposed him in America, and later in the lecture lays out his plan for reform from within and for strength over weakness.

key_terms.sense: professed open-mindedness
tolerance of disagreement, which he says is often only talk
the moment one disagrees, the support is withdrawn

core_teaching: Much professed tolerance is conditional: support lasts only as long as you agree, and disagreement reveals it.

commentaries.who: Surrounding lecture (Complete Works vol. 3)
commentaries.gist: The remark comes right after he rejects the rumour that Theosophists made his American success, and just before he recounts how Theosophists and some missionaries worked against him there.

commentaries.who: Swami Nikhilananda's biography (vivekananda.net)
commentaries.gist: Records that in this lecture he criticised Theosophists who had tried to undermine his work in America and later claimed credit, while noting many Theosophists in India were genuine well-wishers.

commentaries.who: Lecture chronology (vivekananda.net)
commentaries.gist: Dates 'My Plan of Campaign' to 9 February 1897 at the Victoria Public Hall, Madras.

practical_reading: If someone's warmth vanished when you disagreed with them, the change says something about the conditions they placed on it; you need not conclude you were wrong to differ.
misreadings: Not proof that everyone who withdraws after a disagreement was false.
Not encouragement to provoke disagreement to test people.
cautions: Original target is organisations and public critics, not family or partners; applying it to 'someone close' is an extension. Avoid using it to write off a relationship after one quarrel.
speaks_to: hurt from a friend turned critic
not_for: someone whose disagreement involved hurting the other person
a quarrel that may still be repaired
research_note: Setting says 'on friends who turned critics': broadly fair, but the 'friends' were Theosophists and other public supporters.

verified_ref: Nitishatakam 87 (GRETIL 1.87; Wortham 1886 and Kale 1902 also 87); Kosambi 1948 no. 246 (doubtful block).
attribution_note: Kosambi prints it among the doubtful verses (201-352).
translation_note: Our Sanskrit does not match the GRETIL text it cites. GRETIL reads 'kṣīṇo 'py upacīyate punaś candraḥ | ... santapyante na duḥkheṣu' (not consumed in their sorrows); Kosambi reads '... na vidhureṣu' (in misfortunes); Kale's translation ('not troubled in this world when plunged in misery') implies a third reading. Our 'vardhate loke ... na loke 'smin' repeats 'loke' and loses the point that the good are not crushed *by their troubles*. Wortham adds the nuance that they may be distressed but are not overwhelmed. Suggested translation: 'A tree that is cut grows again; the waning moon waxes again. Reflecting on this, good people are not consumed by their misfortunes.'
context: In Wortham's arrangement this verse belongs to the section on the Power of Fate (84-93), not the section on constancy (80-83): it follows the fable of the rat and the starving snake, the ball that bounces back, and the line that idleness is the great enemy, and is followed by Indra's defeat despite all his advantages. It is the hopeful counterweight inside that fate section.

key_terms.sense: a tree, though cut, grows again
the moon, though waned, fills out again
reflecting, keeping this in mind
are not burned up / tormented

core_teaching: Loss and decline in nature are followed by regrowth; remembering this cycle keeps the good from being consumed by their misfortunes, even when they feel them.

commentaries.who: B. Hale Wortham, translation and notes (1886, Niti 87)
commentaries.gist: Wise men reflect thus and, though distressed, are not overwhelmed. Compares Job 14:7 (hope for a cut tree) and Horace's Odes, noting both draw the opposite conclusion for human death: the tree returns, the man does not.

commentaries.who: M. R. Kale, translation and notes (1902 ed., Niti 87)
commentaries.gist: Glosses the verb for the moon as 'waxes, grows in bulk'; good men are not grieved when overpowered by difficulties.

commentaries.who: D. D. Kosambi, critical edition (1948, no. 246)
commentaries.gist: Doubtful-block verse; critical text ends 'na vidhureṣu' (not in adversities).

practical_reading: On a bad day, look for one thing in your life that has already grown back after being cut down; let it remind you that this low phase is a phase.
misreadings: Not a promise that a particular person or relationship will return.
Not 'the wise feel nothing'; they feel it but are not consumed.
cautions: Used in 'someone-left': the renewal image is about fortunes, not people. Wortham's own note points out that Job and Horace apply the same image to say the dead do not return. Do not imply that someone who left or died will come back.
'Good people are not tormented' can sound like a judgement on a reader who is tormented; stress 'not consumed', not 'not affected'.
speaks_to: hope after loss of status or work
not_for: fresh bereavement read as 'they will come back'
someone who needs permission to grieve before hearing about regrowth
research_note: Setting label 'Closing verse of the section on steadfastness' conflicts with Wortham (section on fate). Our prasang 'On steadfastness' also folds in the bouncing ball (85), which Wortham likewise places under fate. Section boundaries differ by edition; GRETIL has no headings.

verified_ref: Bhramargeet-Saar (Ramchandra Shukla's selection from the Sursagar, 1920 onward) pada 316: numbered 316 in both commentary editions checked (Anita Prakashan, Delhi 1977; Narendradev Shastri's tika, Vinod Pustak Mandir, Agra 1957). Opening line(s) only; the full pada has 6 lines.
attribution_note: Speaker 'the gopis' is right. The listener 'a friend' is supported: the pada itself says 'sunu sajani' (listen, friend) and the 1977 commentary opens 'he sakhi'. The last line turns to Krishna directly ('Surdas's Lord, the water has risen, save Gokul'), so the pada moves from a friend to an appeal to Krishna.
translation_note: Faithful to the opening couplet. Our Devanagari ('sada rahati pavas ritu ham pai') matches the 1977 edition. Minor variants between editions in later lines (e.g. 'drig anjan lagat nahin' vs 'anjan thir na rahat'); not used in our excerpt.
context: In the Bhramargeet, Krishna has left Braj for Mathura and sent Uddhav to teach the gopis formless (nirguna) yoga; most padas are the gopis' replies and laments. In this one they describe their own state: since Shyam left the rains never stop; kohl will not stay in their eyes and streaks their cheeks and breasts black; their bodices never dry; and the flood of tears now threatens to drown Gokul, so they ask Krishna to come and save it.

key_terms.sense: eyes raining night and day: unbroken weeping
the monsoon season; here grief that has become a permanent climate
Shyam (Krishna) has gone away; also a pun on the dark rain-cloud (ghanashyam) of the last line
rescue, lift out (of the flood)

core_teaching: Not a doctrine but an expression of viraha (love in separation): the loss of the beloved is so total that weeping becomes a season rather than an event. The bhakti tradition treats such longing as a form of love itself, not something to be fixed.

commentaries.who: Hindi tika in Bhramar Geet-saar (Anita Prakashan, Delhi 1977), pada 316
commentaries.gist: Gopis, weeping day and night in Krishna's absence, compare themselves to the rainy season. Last line read as a plea: the tears have flooded Gokul, so save it as you once did by lifting Govardhan. Praised for its emotion and imagery; figures noted: rupaka, atishayokti, upama.

commentaries.who: Narendradev Shastri, Hindi tika, Bhramar Geetsar (Agra 1957), pada 316
commentaries.gist: Gopis describe their viraha: eyes raining since Krishna left, kohl washed onto cheeks, bodice never dry, Gokul flooding with tears; they ask the Lord to rescue it. Notes rupaka and atishayokti.

commentaries.who: Same edition, introduction (on viraha in Sur)
commentaries.gist: Quotes this pada to show the gopis' tears have not stopped since Krishna went to Mathura, then lists the ten classical stages of viraha that Sur depicts.

commentaries.who: e-PG Pathshala (INFLIBNET) module on Bhramargeet-saar
commentaries.gist: Explains the Saar as Shukla's 1920 selection of about 400 Sursagar padas; viraha drives the whole episode, and the gopis answer Uddhav's yoga with love and gentle reproach rather than debate.

practical_reading: Teachers and singers use it to give grief permission: missing someone can feel like weather that does not lift, and saying so plainly is part of loving them. It names the feeling without asking the reader to stop it.
misreadings: Not a call to stay in tears forever or a judgment that one should be 'over it'; it simply describes how separation feels.
Not about romantic loss only in the tradition: the gopis' longing is read as devotion to Krishna.
cautions: Mentions flooding/drowning as hyperbole for tears; fine for most readers, but keep the gloss gentle.
Imagery of tears soaking the bodice and breasts is in the full pada; our excerpt avoids it.
speaks_to: someone who has left or moved away
longing after a breakup or separation
not_for: a reader who needs reassurance that the pain will end soon (the verse offers none)
contexts where the speaker should be shown moving on
research_note: Kavita Kosh (kavitakosh.org) has this pada but its robots.txt blocks ClaudeBot/anthropic-ai, so it was not used as a source. Both archive.org texts are OCR of copyrighted Hindi commentaries (1957, 1977): paraphrased only.

verified_ref: Bhramargeet-Saar pada 10 (Shukla's selection): numbered 10 in the Anita Prakashan 1977 edition and in Narendradev Shastri's 1957 tika. Our excerpt is lines 1-4 of an 8-line pada.
attribution_note: Speaker Krishna is right. Strictly the pada is spoken to Uddhav as a message to carry to Yashoda (the 1977 commentary: 'he Uddhav, tell mother Yashoda...'), so 'listener: Yashoda' is the intended recipient, not the person present. The setting 'Krishna in Mathura sends a message to his mother' is correct. It is a reply to Yashoda's own message ('I am only your son's nurse, keep showing kindness'), per the 1977 notes.
translation_note: Accurate. 'Warm milk at evening' slightly flattens 'dhaiya/chhaiya': the commentary glosses it as the stream of milk straight from the cow's udder, i.e. fresh milk as only home gives it. 'In four or five days' is glossed as 'soon'.
context: Krishna is in Mathura after killing Kamsa and is sending Uddhav to Braj. Before he goes, Krishna gives him a message for his foster-mother: stay well, we brothers will come soon; since I left no one has called me Kanhaiya, no breakfast, no fresh milk. The rest of the pada asks her to keep his flute and toys safe from Radha and to tell Nand he has been hard-hearted for not sending word. In the story Krishna does not return to live in Braj.

key_terms.sense: stay well, be happy (do not worry about me)
four or five days: idiom for 'soon'
the pet name only his mother and Braj used
morning snack / milk squirted fresh from the udder: the small cares of home

core_teaching: Love in separation runs both ways: Krishna, now a prince, misses the ordinary tenderness of home, a pet name and a mother's food. The commentators use it to show Sur's love is mutual, not only the gopis longing for Krishna.

commentaries.who: Hindi tika in Bhramar Geet-saar (Anita Prakashan, Delhi 1977), pada 10
commentaries.gist: Krishna tells Uddhav to reassure Yashoda. Notes the pada answers critics who say Sur shows only one-sided love: Krishna longs for Nand, Yashoda, Radha, even his toys. The 'Kanhaiya' line shows his ache to hear her pet name again.

commentaries.who: Same edition, notes on the preceding pada
commentaries.gist: Reads this as Krishna's answer to Yashoda's humble message; his promise to come is meant to reassure her that royal splendour has not made him forget Braj.

commentaries.who: Narendradev Shastri, Hindi tika (Agra 1957), pada 10
commentaries.gist: Krishna asks Uddhav to say: let mother be well, we brothers come in four or five days; no one calls me Kanhaiya; keep my flute safe; tell Nand he never sent word after leaving me in Mathura.

practical_reading: For someone living away from parents, it voices what is actually missed: not big things but being called by your home name, being fed. It also models the message home that says 'I am fine, I will come soon' while admitting the ache.
misreadings: Not a promise that a separation will be short; in the story the return does not happen.
Not a complaint against the new place (Mathura): it is about what only home gives.
cautions: The 'four or five days' promise is poignant because Krishna never returns to live in Braj; a reader who has lost a parent may feel this sharply.
For someone estranged from parents, the warm mother image may sting.
speaks_to: living far from parents (study, work, abroad)
missing a parent's small daily care
an adult child who wants to reassure parents
not_for: someone whose parent has died recently (the 'I will come soon' line can wound)
someone estranged from or harmed by a parent
research_note: The NPS Sursagar reads lines 5-6 differently (cited in the 1977 notes); our excerpt (lines 1-4) is unaffected. Commentaries are copyrighted (1957, 1977): paraphrased.

verified_ref: Kabir Granthavali (ed. Shyamsundar Das, Nagari Pracharini Sabha), sakhi 1 of 'Het Preeti Saneh ko Ang' (section 44 'on love and affection'); cited by Hazari Prasad Dwivedi as K. Gr. p. 67. 'Kavita-Kaumudi 66' could not be checked.
attribution_note: Attribution to Kabir is as solid as any Kabir sakhi: it is in the Shyamsundar Das Granthavali (Rajasthani/Dadupanthi manuscript tradition) and quoted by Hazari Prasad Dwivedi. In that context the 'dear one' is the guru or God, not a family member; 'love across distance' fits, 'far-from-parents' is an extension.
translation_note: Meaning correct. Text differs from the Granthavali: first half reads 'kamodani jalahari basai' (lives in the pool/water), and the second 'jo jahi ka bhavata, so tahi ke pas'. Our 'जल में बसै' and 'जो है जाको भावता' are later popular forms (the second appears in sakhi 3 of the same section). 'Always near them' adds 'always'; the original says simply 'is near them'.
context: In Kabir's sakhis grouped under love and affection, this opens the section. The next sakhi says the guru lives in Banaras and the disciple across the sea, yet one with real virtue never forgets; the third says whoever is truly dear will come to you sooner or later, and one you gave body and mind to never leaves. Hazari Prasad Dwivedi quotes the pair to describe Kabir and his guru Ramananda: love does not recognise distance or caste.

key_terms.sense: the night-blooming water lily, which opens to the moon
the one who is dear, who pleases the heart
is near that very one (in the heart, despite distance)

core_teaching: Real love is not measured in distance: the lily in the water and the moon in the sky are far apart yet joined, and whoever is dear to someone stays close to them. In context it is said of guru and disciple, and of God and devotee.

commentaries.who: Pushpapal Singh, Kabir Granthavali Satik (Hindi gloss, 1962)
commentaries.gist: The lily is in water and the moon far away, yet their love stays whole; whoever is someone's beloved is very close even while far. Names the figure as drishtant (illustrative example).

commentaries.who: Hazari Prasad Dwivedi, Kabir (1960 ed.), chapter on outer practice
commentaries.gist: Uses the sakhi of Ramananda and Kabir: love ignores distance, difference and caste; even if the guru were in Banaras and Kabir overseas, the guru's affection would reach him.

commentaries.who: Surrounding sakhis (Kabir Granthavali, ed. Shyamsundar Das, section 44)
commentaries.gist: The section continues: the guru in Banaras, the disciple on the sea-shore, never forgotten; the beloved comes sooner or later; one given body and mind never leaves. Sets the verse in devotional love.

practical_reading: Used today to comfort people separated by distance: closeness is held in the heart, not in kilometres. A reader far from family can treat the bond as already present, and keep it alive by remembering.
misreadings: Not a claim that distance never hurts or that missing someone is a mistake.
In Kabir it is mainly about guru/God; do not present it as a family poem without saying it widens his image.
cautions: For someone separated by death, 'those we love are never far' can feel like a platitude; use gently.
For a reader whose loved one has cut contact, it may sound like denial.
speaks_to: living far from parents or family
not_for: fresh bereavement as a first response
estrangement or rejection by the loved one
research_note: Could not verify 'Kavita-Kaumudi 66' (Ramnaresh Tripathi's anthology): the archive.org volume found was a different part. Kavita Kosh, named in our verified_with, blocks AI agents in robots.txt and was not used. Dwivedi and Pushpapal Singh are under copyright: paraphrased.

verified_ref: Complete Works, Vol. 2, Practical Vedanta and other lectures, 'The Ideal of a Universal Religion'. The CW page gives no venue or date; vivekananda.net's lecture list dates it to New York, 12 January 1896. Page 385 not checked.
translation_note: Passage confirmed in the lecture, in the paragraph beginning 'I have also my little plan'.
context: Vivekananda argues that earlier attempts at religious harmony failed because they tried to boil all religions down to a few shared doctrines, producing more quarrelling sects. His own 'little plan' is not to destroy anyone's faith but to help each person grow along their own line. The child and plant analogy supports this: no one makes another spiritual; a helper can only remove obstacles. He then describes four types of mind (active, emotional, mystical, philosophical) that a universal religion must serve.

key_terms.sense: growth comes from within the learner
the helper's whole role
protection, not manufacture, of growth

core_teaching: Growth, whether a child's or a seeker's, comes from inside; those who help can create opportunities and protect from harm, but cannot force the growing.

commentaries.who: Surrounding lecture (Complete Works vol. 2)
commentaries.gist: The analogy belongs to his argument 'help, do not destroy': stop assuming you can make others spiritual; serve the different types of mind instead of forcing one mould.

commentaries.who: Vedanta Society of Northern California, monthly reading of this lecture
commentaries.gist: Reads the passage as following from his view that God is the centre of all religions and each person moves toward it along a different path, so one should meet people where they are and help them forward.

commentaries.who: Lecture chronology (vivekananda.net)
commentaries.gist: Dates 'The Ideal of a Universal Religion' to New York, 12 January 1896.

practical_reading: For a parent: today, instead of pushing a skill or lesson, remove one obstacle (a distraction, a fear, a missing tool) and give one opportunity, then step back and let the child do the growing.
misreadings: Not 'leave children to it'; providing and protecting is the hedge he describes.
Not a rejection of teaching; it redefines the teacher's job.
cautions: In context it is about spiritual growth; applying it to parenting is a natural but modern extension.
Parents of children with special needs may hear 'the child teaches himself' as dismissive of the support they give; stress the hedge.
speaks_to: trust in a child's own growth
not_for: a parent dealing with a child in danger or crisis, where active intervention is the hedge

verified_ref: Complete Works, Vol. 7, Epistles - Third Series, letter LII, to Mrs Blodgett ('Aunt Roxy'), dated 2 May 1900; the CW page gives no place. Page 525 not checked.
translation_note: Key sentence checked verbatim.
context: Vivekananda tells Mrs Blodgett that after six months of intense work he has relapsed into nervous exhaustion and fever, though his heart and kidneys are sound, and that he will rest a few days in the country before going to Chicago. He mentions introducing Miss Noble, whom he calls his daughter, to a Chicago friend. The closing lines bless her and then admit he badly wants some peace and ask for her prayers.

key_terms.sense: rest from exhaustion and constant demands
a teacher asking for support, not giving it
his affectionate address to his former hostess

core_teaching: Even a great teacher reaches the end of his strength and says so plainly, asking others for help.

commentaries.who: Context of the letter (Complete Works vol. 7, letter LII)
commentaries.gist: Health relapse after six months of lecturing; plans a short country rest before Chicago; arranges for Sister Nivedita's work; ends with the plea for peace and prayers, love to Kate and greetings to friends.

commentaries.who: Vivekananda chronology, May 1900 (vivekananda.net)
commentaries.gist: Places him at Camp Taylor, California, as guest of Alice Hansbrough on 2 May 1900, when he wrote to Mrs Blodgett and to Sister Nivedita.

commentaries.who: Swami Vivekananda in California (Wikipedia)
commentaries.gist: He reached California on 3 December 1899; Roxie Blodgett was among his Los Angeles hosts; he left California for Chicago on 30 May 1900.

practical_reading: If you are running on empty, it is allowed to say it out loud and ask someone to hold you in their thoughts or give you an hour off.
misreadings: Not a sign of spiritual failure; the point is honest need.
cautions: Written by a monk to a friend, not about parenting; its use for parents rests on the shared exhaustion.
not_for: someone who needs practical steps rather than permission to feel tired
research_note: Setting correction: the letter was written from Camp Taylor in northern California; Mrs Blodgett had been his hostess in Los Angeles some months earlier.

verified_ref: Complete Works, Vol. 6, Notes of Class Talks and Lectures, 'On Raja-Yoga' (the closing sentence). The CW page gives no recorder, place or date. Page 89 not checked.
attribution_note: These are notes of a class talk, so the wording may be a note-taker's rather than Vivekananda's own; the sentence is in the Complete Works as printed.
translation_note: Checked verbatim; it is the last line of the page.
context: The short notes sketch the eight limbs of Raja-Yoga: yama (non-injury, truthfulness, non-covetousness, chastity, purity in thought, word and deed), a firm upright seat, about half an hour of breath control with Om repeated mentally, then withdrawal of the senses, concentration, meditation and samadhi. The instruction to do one thing at a time closes the list.

key_terms.sense: holding the mind on one point (concentration)
drawing the senses back from their objects

key_terms.term: whole soul ... to the exclusion of all else
key_terms.sense: complete absorption in the task in hand

core_teaching: Concentration grows by giving one task, while you do it, your full attention, rather than scattering yourself.

commentaries.who: Surrounding notes (Complete Works vol. 6, 'On Raja-Yoga')
commentaries.gist: The line caps a compressed outline of the eight limbs, so it reads as the practical form of concentration (dharana) in daily work.

commentaries.who: Raja-Yoga, 'Pratyahara and Dharana' (Complete Works vol. 1)
commentaries.gist: Makes the same point at length: would-be yogis must stop nibbling at many things, take up one idea and let it fill thought and life; dharana is confining the mind to one point.

practical_reading: Pick the single next task, close everything else for a short block, and give that one task all your attention until the block ends.
misreadings: Not a demand for perfection or hours of unbroken focus.
Not a rule that one may only ever have one project.
cautions: For someone with ADHD or high anxiety, 'to the exclusion of all else' can sound impossible; frame it as a short, kind experiment.
not_for: someone whose difficulty starting comes from depression, where focus advice can add guilt
research_note: Provenance of the CW vol. 6 class notes (recorder, date) not found; plan text should attribute it as 'from notes of a class talk'.

verified_ref: Vairagyashatakam 18 in popular numbering (GRETIL 3.18; Madhavananda 1916 no. 18); Wortham 1886 no. 21; Kale 1902 no. 21; Kosambi 1948 no. 160 (core verse).
translation_note: Good. Minor variant: GRETIL and ours read 'dāhātmyam' (that it burns); Kosambi and Kale read 'māhātmyam' (its power). Meaning is the same.
context: In the Vairagyashatakam's section mocking our failure to give up pleasures. The verse before contrasts Shiva, master of himself even in union with Gauri, with sensualists who can neither enjoy pleasures nor let them go; the verse after says what we call happiness is only the relief of thirst, hunger and lust.

key_terms.sense: the moth (falls) into the blazing fire
meat with a hook in it (bait)
even though we know
desires tangled in a net of dangers
deep / unfathomable is the power of delusion

core_teaching: Unlike the moth and the fish, we see the danger in our cravings and still cling to them; this shows how deep delusion runs, not merely ignorance.

commentaries.who: Swami Madhavananda, translation with notes (1916, no. 18)
commentaries.gist: Renders the insect as not knowing the fire's burning power and the fish as ignorant of the hook, while we, with full discernment, keep desires full of dangers; calls the power of delusion inscrutable. Situates it between verses on Shiva's mastery and on pleasure as mere relief.

commentaries.who: M. R. Kale, translation (1902 ed., Vairagya 21)
commentaries.gist: Moth and fish act through ignorance; we who know better do not give up sense-objects complicated by a net of difficulties; infatuation is mysterious.

commentaries.who: B. Hale Wortham, translation (1886, Vairagya 21)
commentaries.gist: We know the entanglements fortune lays and still keep our desires, wandering in a thicket of error.

commentaries.who: D. D. Kosambi, critical edition (1948, no. 160)
commentaries.gist: Core verse; reads 'māhātmyam'.

practical_reading: Pick one craving you already know is bad for you and name it honestly; knowing is not enough, so add one small practical barrier between you and it.
misreadings: Not a claim that all desire is bad.
Not a reason for self-contempt; the poet includes himself in 'we'.
cautions: Can feed shame for someone struggling with addiction or compulsive behaviour; frame it as a shared human pattern and point to real help where needed.
speaks_to: knowing something is bad for you and doing it anyway
not_for: someone in active addiction crisis as a stand-alone message

verified_ref: Nitishatakam 106 in Wortham 1886 and Kale 1902 numbering, but GRETIL (Chaukhamba) numbers it 1.105 (GRETIL 1.106 is a different verse, on the steadfast man unpierced by love's arrows); Kosambi 1948 no. 226 (doubtful block).
attribution_note: Kosambi prints it among the doubtful verses. Wortham notes a close variant in the Hitopadesha (Suhridbheda 67).
translation_note: Good. 'Kadarthita' covers being despised, afflicted or worried (Kale), so 'harassed' or 'humiliated' both work.
context: Near the end of the Nitishatakam. In Wortham's arrangement the section 'The Praise of Action' runs from 94 to the end (110), and its closing verses praise the dhīra, the steadfast person. The next verse in Wortham/Kale says such a person is not pierced by love's arrows, burned by anger or snared by greed.

key_terms.sense: even of one who is harassed / humiliated
a steadfast character / the quality of steadiness
to wipe away, erase
fire turned face-down
the flame never goes downward

core_teaching: Steadiness that is part of one's nature survives rough treatment, just as a flame keeps rising however the torch is held.

commentaries.who: M. R. Kale, translation and notes (1902 ed., Niti 106)
commentaries.gist: Glosses kadarthita as despised, afflicted, worried; the courage of the heroic cannot be subdued, as a downturned flame does not point to the ground. Discusses Telang's alternative reading.

commentaries.who: B. Hale Wortham, translation and notes (1886, Niti 106)
commentaries.gist: The constant man keeps his virtue in misfortune; notes the Hitopadesha version, where it is the steady person's understanding that is not lost when troubled.

commentaries.who: D. D. Kosambi, critical edition (1948, no. 226)
commentaries.gist: Doubtful-block verse.

practical_reading: After a knock to your confidence, remind yourself of a quality in you that did not change because someone treated you badly; act from it today.
misreadings: Not 'strong people never feel humiliated'.
Not a test the reader is failing if they feel shaken.
cautions: For a reader who feels not good enough, 'the steadfast are unshakeable' can read as proof they are not steadfast; frame the flame as something they already have.
not_for: someone currently being abused, if it implies they should simply endure
research_note: ID/numbering inconsistency: every other bh.niti id follows GRETIL numbering, but this one (106) follows Wortham/Kale; in GRETIL it is 1.105. Setting 'From the section on action' matches Wortham (action section 94-110); Wortham prints his 'Miscellaneous' verses separately after 110.

verified_ref: Nitishatakam 81 in popular numbering (GRETIL 1.81); Wortham 1886 no. 80; Kale 1902 no. 80; Kosambi 1948 no. 52 (core verse).
translation_note: Good. 'Niścitārthāt' is 'from a purpose once settled'; Kale renders it as a policy once determined.
context: Opens the Nitishatakam's section in praise of constancy (Wortham: 'With this sloka begins the section on the praise of firmness'). It recalls the churning of the ocean: the gods kept churning past the precious jewels that surfaced and past the deadly poison until the nectar came up. The next verses describe the steadfast person indifferent to hard ground or soft couch, and unmoved by praise or blame.

key_terms.sense: were not satisfied with priceless jewels
the terrible poison (from the churning)
nectar, the goal of the churning
do not stop short of a settled purpose
the steadfast

core_teaching: The steadfast are neither distracted by early rewards nor scared off by early dangers; they keep going until the real goal is reached.

commentaries.who: M. R. Kale, translation and notes (1902 ed., Niti 80)
commentaries.gist: Explains that thirteen precious things came up before nectar, the fourteenth; points to the churning story in the Ramayana (Bala-kanda) and Bhagavata (book 8).

commentaries.who: B. Hale Wortham, translation and notes (1886, Niti 80)
commentaries.gist: Notes this verse opens the section on firmness; renders the gods as not turned aside by pearls of great price or fear of poison.

commentaries.who: D. D. Kosambi, critical edition (1948, no. 52)
commentaries.gist: Core verse; same text in substance.

practical_reading: When a resolve produces an early win or an early scare, treat both as stages of the churning; ask what the 'nectar' was and keep going toward that.
misreadings: Steadiness is not refusing to reassess a goal.
Not glorifying pushing through genuine danger to health.
cautions: The 'poison' stage can be read as 'ignore warning signs'; keep the reassessment caveat.
speaks_to: not settling for an early partial reward
persisting through a scary middle stage
not_for: someone whose goal is harming them and who needs permission to stop

verified_ref: Complete Works, Vol. 5, Epistles - First Series, letter XLVII, to the Maharaja of Khetri, U.S.A., 9 July 1895 (the online page title misprints it as XLVI). Page 91 not checked.
attribution_note: Genuine Vivekananda letter; the wording is as printed in the Complete Works.
translation_note: Both sentences checked verbatim.
context: Writing from America, Vivekananda reminds the Maharaja that he is persistent: he has started a movement with a few hundred followers, plans to train some sannyasins to carry it on, and says the more the Christian priests oppose him the more determined he is to leave a mark. He plans to go to London by late August and winter between London and New York before returning to India. He then frames opposition as a stage and welcomes it, so long as he stays steady, pure and faithful to God.

key_terms.sense: the three stages he says every work passes through
one who thinks beyond the present will be misunderstood
his condition for welcoming opposition

core_teaching: Resistance is a normal stage of any new work, not a final verdict on it; the task is to stay steady and true while it lasts.

commentaries.who: Context of the letter (Complete Works vol. 5, letter XLVII)
commentaries.gist: The line comes amid practical plans for his American work and a remark that clergy opposition only hardens his resolve; he welcomes persecution on condition that he himself remains pure and faithful.

commentaries.who: Addressee: Ajit Singh of Khetri (Wikipedia)
commentaries.gist: The Maharaja was his patron and close friend who had paid for his journey to the 1893 Parliament, which explains the letter's frank report on progress and setbacks.

practical_reading: If your resolve is being laughed at or resisted, treat that as a stage to pass through; check your own conduct, then keep going.
misreadings: Not proof that opposition means you are right; he pairs it with staying pure and steady.
Not a license to dismiss all criticism as ridicule.
cautions: Can feed grandiosity ('I am ahead of my time'); pair it with honest self-checking.
speaks_to: early resistance to a new habit or project
not_for: someone whose plan is meeting opposition because it harms others

verified_ref: Nitishatakam 53 (GRETIL 1.53; Wortham 1886 and Kale 1902 also 53); Kosambi 1948 no. 27 (core verse). Also in the Hitopadesha (Mitralabha 90, per Wortham) and in Chanakya collections.
attribution_note: A floating gnomic verse: in Kosambi's core Bhartrihari set, but Kale (citing Telang) notes it is also attributed to Chanakya and found in anthologies (Kavyasangraha, Sharngadhara). Safer wording: 'a verse in Bhartrihari's Nitishatakam'.
translation_note: Good. The 'line' ('still bites') is slightly stronger than the verse, which asks whether such a snake is any less frightening; acceptable as paraphrase.
context: Opens the Nitishatakam's portrait of wicked people right after the list of their marks (cruelty, causeless quarrels, envy of the good and of relatives). It is followed by the verse on how the wicked brand every virtue as a vice.

key_terms.sense: a wicked / ill-natured person
to be avoided, kept at a distance
adorned with learning
a snake decorated with a jewel

core_teaching: Talent or learning does not make a harmful person safe; judge people by how they treat others and keep your distance from those who harm.

commentaries.who: M. R. Kale, notes (1902 ed., Niti 53)
commentaries.gist: Explains the old belief that a certain kind of serpent carries a jewel in its crest that shines at night; records Telang's note that the verse is attributed to Chanakya and appears in older anthologies.

commentaries.who: B. Hale Wortham, translation and notes (1886, Niti 53)
commentaries.gist: Renders it plainly (avoid an evil man though learned; a jewelled snake is no less feared) and cross-references the Hitopadesha.

commentaries.who: D. D. Kosambi, critical edition (1948, no. 27)
commentaries.gist: Core verse.

practical_reading: If someone who keeps hurting you is admired for their brilliance or charm, give yourself permission to step back anyway; distance is a reasonable response to harm.
misreadings: It means keeping distance from people who harm you, not labelling everyone who annoys you.
Not contempt for learning or talent.
cautions: If the reader is in an abusive situation, the verse supports distance, but safety planning and support matter more than a verse; include a pointer to help.
speaks_to: a charming or brilliant person who harms you
not_for: ordinary disagreements with decent people
